title: Stylesheet 3D, Grid Lanes, Place Values, Half Seconds & Synthesised Clicks
description: A 3D scene declared as CSS, masonry the browser packs itself, numbers that roll per place, and interface sound with no files.

drops.title: A Stylesheet That Renders 3D
drops.description: Declare an @scene, style it with id rules, animate it with @keyframes — it compiles to one raymarching shader.
drops.concept: GSS takes the most familiar authoring format on the web and points it at a 3D scene: shapes are declared in an @scene block, styled by id selectors with a real cascade, and animated by @keyframes. This reimplementation parses a live-editable sheet and drives a single fragment shader where every declared shape is one signed-distance term — no meshes, no scene graph. Editing the stylesheet changes the scene in the same keystroke.

interaction.mouse: Drag to orbit the camera, wheel to pull the camera in and out.
interaction.click: Switch between three example sheets, or toggle the raymarch cost map to see where the steps go.
interaction.touch: Drag anywhere on the canvas to orbit; the stylesheet editor becomes a full-width drawer.

drops.title: Masonry the Browser Does Itself
drops.description: display: grid-lanes against the JS lane balancer we have all written, with the vertical slack each leaves measured live.
drops.concept: Safari shipped native masonry as display: grid-lanes, so items flow into whichever lane is currently shortest without a line of JavaScript. This demo puts the native property, a hand-written shortest-lane-first balancer, and plain CSS grid side by side, reporting each one's total height, leftover vertical slack, and how many layout measurements it had to take. The native path is declared after a plain grid so unsupported browsers degrade instead of collapsing.
drops.source: Piccalilli — “Native masonry layouts with CSS grid lanes”

interaction.mouse: Hover a card to lift it; drag the lane and gap sliders to re-pack the gallery.
interaction.click: Switch between native grid-lanes, the JS balancer, and plain grid.
interaction.touch: The control panel moves inline above the gallery; all three modes work the same.

drops.title: Numbers That Roll by Place Value
drops.description: Pair two strings from the right and every character becomes a place: the thousands sit still while the hundreds roll.
drops.concept: Crossfading one string into another throws the value away. Torph's insight is that a text change is one animation per place: pair old and new from the right, and each slot either stays put, rolls through the digits between its old and new value, or enters and leaves. Four instances here — a currency total, a ticking clock, a word cycle, and an input field matched by caret position instead of place value — all driven by one spring integrator with live stiffness and stagger.

interaction.mouse: Hit the increment buttons to roll the total; drag stiffness, damping and stagger to re-feel the spring.
interaction.click: Toggle slot outlines to see the per-place boxes, or turn caret matching off and watch typing go wrong.
interaction.touch: Type in the field to morph it live; every control is tap-sized.

drops.title: The Half Second After a Click
drops.description: Reserve space for every state, give deletion a window not a dialog, expect interrupted gestures, roll optimism back honestly.
drops.concept: Interior is a library about the half-second most components abandon. Its rules are made measurable here: a save button that pre-measures all four of its labels so the text beside it never shifts (and reports the shift in pixels when you switch reservation off), a delete that leaves a draining undo ring instead of a dialog, a drag-to-confirm that logs every way a gesture can be cancelled, and an optimistic counter that rolls back and says so when the request fails.

interaction.mouse: Save, delete, drag the knob to the end, like and unlike — the gesture log records every cancellation path.
interaction.click: Flip space reservation, the reserved-box overlay, failure rate, and reduced motion.
interaction.touch: Drag the confirm knob with a finger; releasing early or sliding off springs it back.

drops.title: Components That Make Their Own Sound
drops.description: Twelve interface sounds, zero audio files — oscillators and an envelope, re-tunable at runtime.
drops.concept: Bencho ships its interface sounds as code rather than a folder of WAVs, which means they never 404, never wait on a download, and can be re-pitched live. Each sound here is a recipe object — waveform, frequency, sweep target, decay, a dash of noise for the click transient — and the components voice themselves: a toggle that rises and falls a fifth apart, a stepper pitched to its value with an audible end of range, tabs quieter than the confirm chime, and an error a minor second down. AudioContext is built on the first gesture, never on load.

interaction.mouse: Press the arm button once, then every control plays its own voice; the scope shows the waveform.
interaction.click: Audition all twelve recipes from the kit, or re-tune and mute from the panel.
interaction.touch: The first tap arms the audio context, exactly as mobile autoplay policy requires.
